meta.title: Digital Exhibition — Headless Migration
meta.subtitle: Nuxt front-end on linux3 + slimmed WordPress backend
meta.client: TU/e — Built Environment, Digital Exhibition platform
meta.author: marco@tech-paw.com
meta.summary: Move Digital Exhibition to a headless architecture: a Nuxt 3 / Vue / Tailwind front-end that reads the existing WordPress REST API, while the WordPress install on the TU/e server is stripped back to a lean content API. The app was first built and previewed on Cloudflare; that address stays as a preview. It now runs on the TU/e server (linux3, Plesk) at live.digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl: GitHub builds it and the server only downloads the finished files. Pressing Deploy Frontend in WordPress starts the build and linux3 updates by itself. The Cloudflare R2 bucket is used for development only (staging); live keeps its images on its own server. Both the WordPress backend (wp-content) and the front-end are under Git. Still to do: switch the two addresses, the search and replace in the database, and the email.

workstreams.name: Nuxt front-end
workstreams.goal: A production Nuxt 3 front-end that renders the whole Digital Exhibition from the WordPress REST API, with no upstream host or CORS exposed to the browser. It was previewed on Cloudflare and is served from linux3 (see workstream 7).
workstreams.context: Lives in frontend/digital-exhibition, in its own Git repository. Every route — pages, archives, every entry and the home page — is pre-rendered at build time; the home hero is picked in the browser on each visit. Site identity, menus and archive layout are read from WordPress (GET /wp-json/cd/v1/site). A build fails if WordPress can't answer, so the previous complete deployment stays live. Only a few endpoints run at request time: the PDF proxy, the contact form, search and the site settings.

tasks.title: Cloudflare deploy (static assets) + build trigger
tasks.notes: Pre-rendered pages are served as static assets (wrangler.jsonc); the Worker only runs for /api/*. Rebuilds start from WordPress with the Deploy Frontend button (Cloudflare deploy hook). Prerender concurrency is 1, with retries and a warm-up request, because the upstream host drops HTTP/2 streams under parallel load. Cloudflare is now only a preview of the app: the live app runs on linux3 (see 7.1–7.5).

tasks.title: Runtime config & env for prod (WP_API_BASE, WP_SITE_URL)
tasks.notes: WP_API_BASE, WP_SITE_URL and the NUXT_PUBLIC_* values are environment variables; no domain is hardcoded. Point them at staging until the merge, then at live. The build now reads the live WordPress (see 7.6).

tasks.title: Error states, 404, slow-upstream resilience pass
tasks.notes: Verified — error.vue renders a generic statusCode/statusMessage page; [...slug].vue throws a real 404 for unresolved permalinks; EntryView falls back to excerpt + link-out when content.rendered is empty; server/api/wp/[...path].ts retries (3x) with a 30s timeout against the upstream; nitro prerender failOnError:false confirmed.

tasks.title: Cross-browser + mobile QA against the live site
tasks.notes: Cross-browser and mobile QA completed.

tasks.title: Static, settings-driven build
tasks.notes: Site identity, menus and archive definitions come from WordPress (cd/v1/site) and are used to discover and pre-render every route. Builds fail when required data is missing (PRERENDER_REQUIRE_WP). Logos and icon load from WordPress with bundled fallbacks; legacy URLs redirect; R2 upload paths are normalised in the rendered HTML.

tasks.title: Search page + route-fetch resilience
tasks.notes: The search page is pre-rendered and its results render in the browser. WordPress route fetching retries in smaller paginated requests, with clearer errors and longer timeouts for cold starts.

workstreams.name: Slim the TU/e WordPress server
workstreams.goal: Reduce the WordPress install on the TU/e server to what a content API actually needs — no front-end theme rendering weight, no dead code.
workstreams.context: backend/ holds a full WP core + wp-content. The front-end no longer needs WP to render pages for humans, only JSON (plus the Elementor single-region fallback).

tasks.title: Inventory the server: disk, plugins, themes, uploads size
tasks.notes: du -sh wp-content/*, list active vs inactive plugins, DB size, PHP version.

tasks.title: Identify 'useless folder' — the redundant LAMP-stack backend dir
tasks.notes: User flagged a leftover folder used for a local LAMP backend of WP. Confirm it is not referenced by wp-config.php / .htaccess, back it up, remove it.

tasks.title: Remove unused themes, keep one — and rename it
tasks.notes: Done — chique, chique-pro and twentytwentyfive removed; only the active theme is kept. On live the theme was renamed (tue-digital-exhibition) so it is no longer connected to the WordPress theme repository and automatic updates can't replace it. Staging keeps the old name until the merge.

tasks.title: Deactivate + delete confirmed-unused plugins
tasks.notes: Unused plugins removed. No longer installed: wordpress-importer, show-current-template, disable-wp-rest-api. WPForms Lite was deleted. better-search-replace stays until the staging→live merge; post-type-switcher stays while content is still being re-typed.

tasks.title: Document the final server layout in backend/README
tasks.notes: Done — backend/README explains what Git tracks and what it doesn't, and that third-party plugins are not tracked (each server keeps its own). It holds no secrets: credentials live only in wp-config.php, which is not tracked; the repository carries a placeholder (wp-config.reference.php).

tasks.title: Deploy Frontend: confirmation + live build progress
tasks.notes: The admin-bar button asks for confirmation, then follows the build (GitHub, then linux3) until the new version is live. The sticky Preview Changes button was removed and the admin sidebar now lists the day-to-day items first.

tasks.title: Site configuration REST endpoint (cd/v1/site)
tasks.notes: Exposes site identity, menus, footer details and archive configuration to the headless front-end. Part of the custom_dashboard plugin.

tasks.title: Media library: video support
tasks.notes: An ACF video file field plus a safe backfill script; selected uploads play in a native video player, and embeds still work.

tasks.title: PDF field + thumbnail regeneration with R2
tasks.notes: An ACF PDF file field, with legacy dFlip shortcodes backfilled into it. Thumbnails regenerate correctly alongside the media offloader (advmo-regenerate-thumbnails-compat).

workstreams.name: WordPress audit & plugin rationalisation
workstreams.goal: Decide, plugin by plugin, what stays, what is replaced, and what is removed — without touching the two heavy dependencies the content genuinely relies on.
workstreams.context: The plugins we use today are listed in the plugin audit below. Two heavy dependencies the content relies on and that we do not touch: ACF PRO and Elementor / Elementor Pro.

tasks.title: FileBird Pro → open replacement
tasks.notes: Replaced by Figuro Media, our own folder plugin. Folder assignments carried over: 438 folders and 3,943 files imported from FileBird.

tasks.title: DearFlip (dflip) → keep
tasks.notes: Decision: keep the plugin. The front-end self-hosts the dFlip assets (public/dflip) and streams PDFs through its own proxy (useDflip, server/api/pdf).

tasks.title: Keep — Advanced Custom Fields PRO (do not touch)
tasks.notes: Field data drives the REST payloads the front-end consumes. No change. Confirm ACF-to-REST exposure is on for the fields the front-end reads.

tasks.title: Keep — Elementor + Elementor Pro (do not touch)
tasks.notes: 2025–2026 batch of post/courses/seminars is authored in Elementor; content.rendered is empty for those and the front-end lifts elementor-location-single from the rendered page. Removing Elementor breaks that batch.

tasks.title: WP Toolkit — used live, important
tasks.notes: The live site uses WP Toolkit to manage the website and to apply updates and security fixes, so it matters.

tasks.title: Comments — Deleted
tasks.notes: To do: delete comments site-wide (switch the setting off and close existing threads). No plugin needed.

tasks.title: Decide — WordPress mail: FluentSMTP on live, via TU/e's Microsoft mail
tasks.notes: Waiting for TU/e to fix the Microsoft mail. Live will then use FluentSMTP (already installed on live) to send WordPress mail such as password resets; Brevo (free plan, 300 emails a day) remains the alternative. The front-end contact form needs the same decision (see 4.4).

tasks.title: Decide — custom_dashboard / show-current-template / post-type-switcher
tasks.notes: custom_dashboard is our own plugin and stays (Manage News, Quick Actions, Audit Content). post-type-switcher stays only while content is still being re-typed. show-current-template is no longer installed.

tasks.title: Ultimate Addons for Elementor (UAE) — keep
tasks.notes: The plugin folder is header-footer-elementor. Decision: keep it.

tasks.title: Decide — Yoast SEO (wordpress-seo)
tasks.notes: Confirmed yoast_head_json is in the REST output and consumed by the front-end. Yoast now only stores per-entry meta; all rendering is front-end. Title templates still worth tidying in Yoast (some double up the site name).

tasks.title: WPForms Lite — deleted
tasks.notes: Deleted. Forms are handled by the front-end contact form, not by this plugin.

tasks.title: WP Umbrella — kept as it is
tasks.notes: Kept as it is on live, together with the must-use file it loads (InitUmbrella.php). Nothing to change.

workstreams.name: Assets, domain, staging & mail
workstreams.goal: Media on an R2 bucket for development (staging) while live keeps its files local, the domain for the app, a safe staging copy of the WordPress site, and transactional mail.

tasks.title: Move images & PDFs to R2
tasks.notes: Advanced Media Offloader sends uploads to a Cloudflare R2 bucket. It is used on staging only, for development: live keeps every image and PDF on its own server, and the app reads media from the live WordPress. The staging uploads folder was deleted, so staging reads only from R2.

tasks.title: Hosting and domain for the app → linux3
tasks.notes: Decision made: the app is hosted on linux3 (the TU/e server), not on Cloudflare. It already runs at live.digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl. Final layout: digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl shows the app; live. and staging. hold the two WordPress sites. The switch itself is task 7.11.

tasks.title: Stand up a staging environment of the current WP site
tasks.notes: Staging has two jobs: testing new functions on the WordPress site and, in an emergency, replicating live to test the site or find errors. The staging and production databases are not synchronised, but both are up to date.

tasks.title: Transactional mail from the front-end (contact form)
tasks.notes: The contact form is built (components/ContactForm.vue + server/api/contact.post.ts, with validation and honeypot). The handler only logs: no mail is sent, because the Brevo call is still a marked TODO in the code, even if a key is set. Open: which account sends it (the same Microsoft mail as WordPress, or Brevo). Waiting on TU/e.

tasks.title: R2 lifecycle / caching / cost check
tasks.notes: Cache-Control on R2 objects, Cloudflare cache rules, confirm the use can stays in free tier, document the re-sync procedure for new uploads. R2 is now used by staging only.

workstreams.name: SEO on the front-end
workstreams.goal: The Nuxt front-end owns all discoverability: per-page meta, Open Graph, structured data, sitemap, robots — sourced from Yoast fields via REST.
workstreams.context: Indexing is on: the front-end is indexable (robots.txt, meta robots and the sitemap are open). Canonical addresses follow NUXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL, which changes at the address switch.

tasks.title: Per-route meta from yoast_head_json
tasks.notes: Implemented — utils/seo.ts maps yoast_head_json → title/description/canonical/OG/Twitter; composables/useSeo.ts wires it via useHead. Verified against /privacy-policy/, /contact/, entries.

tasks.title: Structured data (JSON-LD)
tasks.notes: Implemented — Yoast's schema @graph is passed through with WP-origin URLs rewritten to the public host; home feed emits a hand-written WebSite + Organization graph.

tasks.title: Dynamic sitemap.xml
tasks.notes: Implemented — server/routes/sitemap.xml.ts enumerates pages + archives + all entries from the proxy (161 URLs). 404s while not indexable.

tasks.title: Canonical strategy: switch to the real domain
tasks.notes: utils/seo.rewriteOrigin() already rewrites every WordPress URL (canonical, og:url, schema) to NUXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL. At go-live set that to digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl, in the build workflow (it is live.digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl for now).

tasks.title: Lift noindex
tasks.notes: Done: the app is indexable. NUXT_PUBLIC_INDEXABLE is true in the build workflow, so every route is indexable, the structured data is emitted and the sitemap is served.

tasks.title: Social / link-preview cards (OG image on a served host)
tasks.notes: buildSeoHead now sends page URLs (canonical/og:url/JSON-LD) to the front-end host but keeps /wp-content media URLs on public.mediaUrl (the live WordPress server) so og:image never 404s. og:image:secure_url/type/alt + twitter:image:alt added. public/robots.txt allow-lists facebookexternalhit / Twitterbot / LinkedInBot / Slackbot / WhatsApp / etc. so shared links render a card. Note: _headers is a Cloudflare Pages file — no effect on linux3.

workstreams.name: Version control (backend + front-end)
workstreams.goal: Put the WordPress backend (wp-content) and the front-end under Git. The backend is merged into live by hand after a check on staging; the front-end is built and published by a GitHub pipeline.
workstreams.context: Git is connected to the server's control panel, so files are merged manually; Git is the version history and the backup. The front-end has its own repository, built by GitHub Actions and deployed to linux3 (see workstream 7).

tasks.title: Initialise a Git repo for wp-content
tasks.notes: Done — git repo initialised in backend/. .gitignore excludes wp-config.php (secrets), *.log, WP upgrade-temp dirs, compressx logs. wp-config.reference.php + README.md added.

tasks.title: Decide what version control tracks
tasks.notes: Tracked: our own code only — the figuro-folder, custom_dashboard and frontend-deploy plugins, the active theme, mu-plugins and maintenance files. Third-party plugins are git-ignored: each server keeps its own. WordPress core, wp-config.php, logs and uploads are not tracked.

tasks.title: Host the repo on GitHub
tasks.notes: Done — pushed to github.com/orso081980/digitalexhibition-backend, branch main, initial commit 35c6d25 (~13.8k files). Switched from private to public visibility per request.

tasks.title: Staging → production by manual merge (backend)
tasks.notes: Done for the code: the staging line (main) was merged into live, main wins, and the old live state is kept under a Git tag. Both sites now follow the same branch. The databases were not merged: live's database is changed only by running the migration scripts in bin/, by hand. The remaining step is the address switch (7.11 and 7.12).

tasks.title: Version control for the front-end
tasks.notes: The Nuxt app has its own Git repository (private on GitHub). GitHub Actions builds the app from it, and the Deploy Frontend button in WordPress starts a new build.

workstreams.name: The app on linux3 + automatic deploy
workstreams.goal: Move the app from Cloudflare to linux3 (the TU/e server), build it on GitHub, and make the Deploy Frontend button update the site by itself.
workstreams.context: Added in two extra days (8 and 9), done over the weekend of 21–22 November so that visitors were not affected. The app repository now has three branches: main (the Cloudflare version, kept as a preview), linux (the source code and the GitHub pipeline) and linux-deploy (only the finished build, which linux3 downloads).

tasks.title: Hosting decision: the app runs on linux3, not Cloudflare
tasks.notes: The app is hosted on the TU/e server (linux3, Plesk). The Cloudflare address stays as a preview of the app, and the R2 bucket is kept for staging (development) only. Live keeps its images on its own server.

tasks.title: Node.js application in Plesk at live.digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl
tasks.notes: A Plesk Node.js app in production mode, with the domain's folder as application root and an empty document root (public), so every request goes through the app. The startup file is app.cjs. The app restarts when tmp/restart.txt changes.

tasks.title: Two new branches in the app repository: linux and linux-deploy
tasks.notes: linux holds the source code and the GitHub workflow; linux-deploy holds only the finished build, one commit per build. There are two because the building happens on GitHub: linux3 only needs the result, so nothing is built (or can break) on the server.

tasks.title: GitHub Actions pipeline: build and publish
tasks.notes: On every push to linux, or on request, GitHub builds the site (5–10 minutes: it reads every page from WordPress) and publishes the files to linux-deploy. If WordPress can't be read the build fails and nothing is published, so a broken build never replaces the running site. The addresses are set in the workflow file; the mail secrets are not stored in Git but in Plesk.

tasks.title: Plesk pulls linux-deploy automatically
tasks.notes: Plesk Git follows linux-deploy with deployment mode Automatic, into the app's folder. Every build carries a fresh tmp/restart.txt, so the app restarts on the new files by itself.

tasks.title: The build reads the live WordPress
tasks.notes: Content now comes from the live WordPress (digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl) instead of staging, and media is served from the same host, with no R2. Indexing for search engines is already on.

tasks.title: Merge the staging code into live (main → live)
tasks.notes: The WordPress code of staging became the live branch. Files managed by the host (WP Toolkit, WP Health, the maintenance page) were left as on live, and so were the live-only plugins. The R2 pieces stay inactive on live: they only switch on when an R2 setting exists in wp-config, which live does not have.

tasks.title: Deploy Frontend plugin starts the GitHub build
tasks.notes: The plugin that was called Cloudflare Deploy Trigger is now Frontend Deploy, with all the Cloudflare code removed. The button starts the GitHub workflow through GitHub's API, with a token limited to that one repository. Settings → Deploy Frontend holds the workflow address, the token, the branch, the app address and the Plesk address.

tasks.title: Automatic pull on linux3: WordPress calls Plesk
tasks.notes: GitHub cannot reach Plesk's webhook from outside (the panel's port is closed to the internet), and SSH was not wanted. WordPress runs on the same server, so after the button is pressed it calls Plesk's webhook locally: first after about two minutes, then every 30 seconds until the new build is live. The settings page shows the result of the last call. No manual 'Pull' in Plesk anymore.

tasks.title: End-to-end test: button → GitHub → linux3
tasks.notes: Pressing Deploy Frontend started the GitHub build; the result was published to linux-deploy and deployed by Plesk without any manual step. The app's build number changed and a course created minutes before pressing the button was on the new site.

tasks.title: Switch the addresses
tasks.notes: The app takes digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl and WordPress live moves to live.digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl. Then the build reads WordPress at its new address, and NUXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL becomes the final address (task 5.4).

tasks.title: Search and replace in the database for the new WordPress address
tasks.notes: Every stored address in the WordPress database changes from digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl to live.digitalexhibition.arch.tue.nl, after a database backup and a dry run (Better Search Replace is installed for this).

architecture.before: Browser → WordPress (Elementor theme renders HTML) on TU/e LAMP box. Media, mail, SEO all inside WP.
architecture.after: Browser → linux3 (Plesk: the Nuxt app, pre-rendered pages served by a small Node.js app; only /api/* runs per request) → /api/wp proxy → WordPress REST API (content source only). A GitHub pipeline builds the app and publishes it to the linux-deploy branch, which linux3 pulls. Media stays on the WordPress server; the R2 bucket is used on staging only. Mail → TU/e's Microsoft mail through FluentSMTP on WordPress; the app's contact form still needs its mail connection. SEO and layout owned by Nuxt. The Cloudflare address remains as a preview.
